Q: No module named pkg_resources A:

just reinstall your setuptools by:

$ sudo wget https://pypi.python.org/packages/source/s/setuptools/setuptools-0.6c11.tar.gz#md5=7df2a529a074f613b509fb44feefefe74e
$ tar -zxvf setuptools-0.6c11.tar.gz
$ cd setuptools-0.6c11/
$ sudo python setup.py build
$ sudo python setup.py install
$ sudo pip install --upgrade setuptools

then everything will be fine.

Q: Carrier in Cyber Security? A:

Step 1: Understand what the threats are

Don't think purely technically at this stage, but conceptually. Security threats include

  • malicious inputs triggering undesired actions
  • forging requests
  • identity theft
  • distributed denial of service
  • careless software use by humans
  • backdoors (including the AI use in fashion, people unwittingly leak private credentials and business secrets when they ask the AI)
  • unhashed passwords

You need to have a knack on technology and programming, but they are not your focus at this stage. Just what the threats are.

Make a document for yourself, have a chapter of all these threats and have a subchapter for all chapters where you describe in your words for yourself what the threat consists of. Avoid technical details at this stage, look at the big picture.

Step 2: Reread your notest described in Step 1 twice, let it sink in, you will rely on this understanding heavily

Step 3: Technical understanding of what the threats are

Now go through your notes, where each main chapter is a separate threat and carefully study each threat on a technical level, with case-studies and make sure you understand why they work and why they are a threat.

Now, write a second subchapter for each of your chapters with technicalities of the threat itself. Don't delve in to how you need to protect a system from such threats, save that for later. Now you need to understand what you need to protect your system from.

Step 4: Once you have written the second subchapter of each chapter, reread your notes, all chapters, describing what the threats are and what their technical description and case studies. Let this sink in

Step 5: Protection

Go to each of your chapters and study the ways to protect the system from those chapters. Write a third subchapter to each of your chapters with describing how to protect against any given threat.

Step 6: Reread your document. Now you have theoretical understanding as well as case studies both for the threats and protection from those

Step 7: Practice

Write some small applications that are secure from the threats you know about.

Step 8: Useful habits

Always refresh software versions to get security fixes and always to stable versions, don't use experimental versions, those may have unexplored security flaws.

Find websites and news dealing with security, read about them, get a habit of making yourself up to date.

Step 9: Deep water

Now that you reached to a pretty good level of knowledge, practice in the wild. Look into open-source projects and find security issues. Find software that auto-detects certain kinds of security flaws and decide what's useful for you, perhaps implement some tools on your own if you are not satisfied with what's on offer.

Q: How to sort my Docker images by size with `docker images` command? A:

Accepted answer doesn't work for me as SIZE is printed as two words - size and unit (MB/GB). The following answer works by concatenating them into a single word and then uses sort -h to properly sort them by size.

docker image list \
| while read -r A B C D E F G H; do \
    { printf '%s\t' "$A" "$B" "$C" "$D" "$E" "$F" "$G$H"; echo; }; \
  done \
| sort -k 7 -h \
| column -t

which can be wrapped into an alias:

alias dils='docker image list | while read -r A B C D E F G H; do { printf '%s\t' "$A" "$B" "$C" "$D" "$E" "$F" "$G$H"; echo; }; done | sort -h -k 7 | column -t'

Q: Why does `\\"` inside a string still result in `\"` after parsing? A:

You’re using single quotes to wrap the string, so escaping double quotes isn’t necessary.

In this case, When the JavaScript engine encounters \\", it resolves \\ into a literal \, and the " is treated as a normal character.

Q: Why Java Byte[] to Int/Int to Byte[] need operation "&0xFF" A:

What does & 0xFF do?

In Java, byte is a signed integral type. That means it can represent negative numbers as well as positive. It's why the value range of byte is [-128, 127] instead of [0, 255]. And the way Java represents signed integral types is with two's complement.

For example, if you have byte b = -2; then the binary representation of b would be:

11111110

Doing b & 0xFF then does two things:

  1. It first promotes b to an int. This is a widening conversion, which for signed integral types involves sign extension.

  2. It performs the bitwise AND operation on the two operands: (int) b and 0xFF. Note the 0xFF is an int literal and is the hexadecimal representation of 255 (in decimal). The leading zeros are implied: 0x000000FF.

In binary, that would look like:

  11111111 11111111 11111111 11111110 // -2 as a 32-bit int
& 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111 // 0x000000FF
―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――
  00000000 00000000 00000000 11111110

The result in decimal is 254 and is the unsigned value of b. In other words, doing b & 0xFF for a given byte b will give you the unsigned value of b as an int. You'll always end up with an int in the range [0, 255].

Note int is also signed. If you want the unsigned value of an int then you need to store it in a long and do & 0xFFFFFFFFL (the L tells Java the literal is a long). That gives you the unsigned value of the int for the same reason & 0xFF gives the unsigned value of a byte. And of course, long is signed as well. But there's no integral primitive large enough to hold the unsigned value of a long, so if you need that then you'd have to move to BigInteger or similar.

Converting byte[4] to int

When converting a byte[4] into an int you need to use the unsigned byte values because you don't want the leading 1 bits of a negative number when bit shifting. Let's say you have 42,117,314 in a byte array:

// 42,117,314
byte[] b = {2, -125, -109, 34};

You would convert that array into an int like so:

int b0 = (b[0] & 0xFF) << 24;
int b1 = (b[1] & 0xFF) << 16;
int b2 = (b[2] & 0xFF) <<  8;
int b3 = (b[3] & 0xFF);
int i  = b0 | b1 | b2 | b3; // 42,177,314

Which in binary would look like:

  (00000000 00000000 00000000 00000010 & 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111) << 24
| (11111111 11111111 11111111 10000011 & 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111) << 16
| (11111111 11111111 11111111 10010011 & 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111) <<  8
| (00000000 00000000 00000000 00100010 & 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111)

=>

  (00000000 00000000 00000000 00000010) << 24
| (00000000 00000000 00000000 10000011) << 16
| (00000000 00000000 00000000 10010011) <<  8
| (00000000 00000000 00000000 00100010)

=>

  00000010 00000000 00000000 00000000
| 00000000 10000011 00000000 00000000
| 00000000 00000000 10010011 00000000
| 00000000 00000000 00000000 00100010
―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――
  00000010 10000011 10010011 00100010

The result is the binary representation of 42,177,314, which is the correct value.

If you didn't include the & 0xFF then the leading 1 bits of the negative bytes would remain, and you'd ultimately end up with (after shifting):

  00000010 00000000 00000000 00000000
| 11111111 10000011 00000000 00000000
| 11111111 11111111 10010011 00000000
| 00000000 00000000 00000000 00100010
―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――
  11111111 11111111 10010011 00100010

The result is now the binary representation of -27,870, which is the incorrect value.

Note the widening of byte to int mentioned earlier happens with all arithmetic, bitwise, and shift operators. So, even without the & 0xFF the byte will be promoted to int and have its sign extended because of the << or | operation, or simply due to assigning it to an int variable (implicit casting).

Converting int to byte[4]

In this case you don't actually need to do & 0xFF because casting to byte is a narrowing conversion, which for signed integral types simply discards the leading bits that don't fit in the smaller type. In other words, casting an int to a byte drops the first 24 bits and keeps the last 8 bits. Thus, the following two expressions give the same result:

// Where 'i' is some 'int'
(byte) (i & 0xFF)
(byte) i

Which means the following will give the expected results:

public static byte[] toBytes(int i) {
  byte[] b = new byte[4];
  b[0] = (byte) (i >> 24);
  b[1] = (byte) (i >> 16);
  b[2] = (byte) (i >>  8);
  b[3] = (byte) i;
  return b;
}

Simplified Implementation

I suspect you're learning, and so doing the bit masking and shifting yourself is educational. However, as noted in this answer, you can use java.nio.ByteBuffer to do these conversions for you. For example:

public static int toInt(byte[] b) {
  // This implementation only takes the first 4 bytes of 'b' into account. It
  // will throw BufferUnderflowException if b.length < 4.
  return ByteBuffer.wrap(b).getInt();
}

public static byte[] toBytes(int i) {
  return ByteBuffer.allocate(4).putInt(i).array();
}

Using ByteBuffer also makes it easier to change the byte order between big and little endian, as needed. The above example always uses big endian.

ByteBuffer has methods for working with short (2 bytes) and long (8 bytes) as well.
